title: VASOTEC (enalapril maleate) tablets: prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 15, effective 23 January 2026, label text Rev. 11/2025
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Bausch Health US, LLC.
result: Boxed warning, fetal toxicity: discontinue as soon as pregnancy is detected; oligohydramnios may not appear until after the fetus has sustained irreversible injury; most epidemiological studies of first-trimester exposure have not distinguished renin-angiotensin drugs from other antihypertensives. Warnings: anaphylactoid and related reactions, presumably because ACE inhibitors affect the metabolism of eicosanoids and polypeptides including endogenous bradykinin; head and neck angio-oedema at any time during treatment, which with laryngeal oedema may be fatal, with higher incidence in Black than non-Black patients and increased risk with mTOR inhibitors (temsirolimus, sirolimus, everolimus) or a neprilysin inhibitor; intestinal angio-oedema presenting as abdominal pain with normal C1 esterase levels, resolving after stopping; life-threatening anaphylactoid reactions during hymenoptera venom desensitisation, and anaphylactoid reactions during dialysis with high-flux membranes and during LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate; excessive hypotension, sometimes with oliguria, progressive azotaemia and rarely acute renal failure or death, in heart failure, hyponatraemia, high-dose diuretic therapy, dialysis or volume depletion, and myocardial infarction or stroke from an excessive fall in pressure in ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease; neutropenia or agranulocytosis, for which trial data are insufficient to exclude a captopril-like rate; rarely a syndrome beginning with cholestatic jaundice that progresses to fulminant hepatic necrosis and sometimes death, by an unknown mechanism. In hypertensive patients with unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis, blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine rose in 20%, almost always reversibly on discontinuation. Hyperkalaemia above 5.7 mEq/l in about 1% of hypertensive patients (discontinuation in 0.28%) and 3.8% in heart failure. NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors given with ACE inhibitors to elderly, volume-depleted or renally impaired patients may cause deterioration of renal function including acute renal failure, usually reversible. Dual blockade with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers or aliskiren raises the risks of hypotension, hyperkalaemia and acute renal failure without additional benefit for most patients. Lithium toxicity has been reported, and nitritoid reactions (flushing, nausea, vomiting, hypotension) with injectable gold. Post-marketing and uncommon trial reports include cardiac arrest, pancreatitis, hepatitis, hepatic failure, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, bone marrow depression, exfoliative dermatitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigus, renal failure and hyponatraemia. Hypotension in heart failure 6.7% and syncope 2.2%; in hypertension 0.9% and 0.5%. Discontinuation for adverse experiences 3.3% in hypertension and 5.7% in heart failure. Mean haemoglobin fell by about 0.3 g/dl; haemolytic anaemia, including in G6PD deficiency, has been reported. Cough is presumed to follow inhibition of bradykinin degradation and always resolves after discontinuation. SOLVD-Treatment: 2569 patients with symptomatic heart failure and ejection fraction of 35% or less followed for up to 55 months; enalapril was associated with an 11% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 30% reduction in heart-failure hospitalisation. SOLVD-Prevention: 4228 patients with ejection fraction of 35% or less without symptomatic heart failure followed for up to 5 years; no statistically significant mortality effect, 32% fewer first heart-failure hospitalisations; the trial was not designed to show whether treating asymptomatic patients is superior to close follow-up with enalapril at the earliest sign of heart failure. CONSENSUS, NYHA class IV heart failure: one-year survival 64% with enalapril (n=127) against 48% with placebo (n=126). Abrupt withdrawal has not been associated with a rapid increase in blood pressure.
